The UPM section states three distinct earned-income-disregard branches with concrete numeric schedules — (B.1) $65.00/month plus 1/2 of remaining income for applicants to the disabled/aged and certain aged recipients; (B.2) $65.00/month plus 1/2 of income remaining after impairment-related expenses for disabled recipients and certain aged recipients; (B.3) $85.00/month plus 1/2 of remaining income for blind applicants/recipients and certain aged recipients — plus the (A) long-term-care-facility exclusion where gross earned income is counted in full. Dropping 100% of this operative content is a whole-rule-fidelity failure and a total semantic collapse of three distinct branches into nothing.

The `status: upstream_source_check_required` deferral is not a legitimate fidelity-preserving fallback for this slice. The disregard amounts are stated explicitly and are computable from the slice alone, with no dependency on any external or higher authority to be understood or applied; 'no higher-authority statute/regulation provided to check' is a verification/process concern, not an encodability barrier. It matches none of the recognized acceptable fallbacks (editorial omission with no operative content, genuinely unsupported ontology, or unavailable subject-to cross-reference), and the ontology here (assistance unit, earned income, aged/blind/disabled status, LTC residence, impairment-related expenses) is entirely ordinary. [non-blocking] Entity is TaxUnit, while 26 USC 32(c)(2)(B)(i) frames earned income as that 'of an individual' and all components (wages, SE earnings, pension, penal-institution service, etc.) are person-level concepts. The ontology is internally coherent (every rule, input, and test uses TaxUnit) and plausible for the EITC aggregate where the (B)(vi) election is a return-level choice, but Person with a tax-unit aggregation may be the more faithful modeling.

[non-blocking] 26 USC 32(c)(2)(B)(i) ('computed without regard to any community property laws') is cited in the source attribution '(B)(i)-(v)' and acknowledged in the summary docstring, but has no explicit formula element. This is defensible because it is a negative computational instruction satisfied by construction (no community-property split is applied to the income inputs), yet the source attribution claims a clause that is only handled implicitly.

[non-blocking] Net earnings from self-employment (section 1402(a), determined with regard to the section 164(f) deduction), section 871(a) nonresident-alien amounts, and section 407(d)(4)/(7) SSA work-activity amounts are modeled as local inputs rather than canonical imports. This is acceptable if those encodings are unavailable in the workspace, and the 164(f) and 'subsidized' qualifiers are faithfully captured in the variable names, but importing from the cited sections would be preferable where available.

[non-blocking] Visible tests confirm the election=false path and the inclusion/exclusion arithmetic, but a test exercising the section 32(c)(2)(B)(vi) election=true branch (section 112 excluded amounts flowing into earned income) is not confirmed because the companion test file is truncated.

[non-blocking] The `max(0, ...)` floor in `earned_income_before_section_112_election` is not stated in 26 USC 32(c)(2); the statutory definition is a pure sum-and-subtract with no explicit zero floor. The effect is immaterial in most cases (negative earned income is bounded downstream in the EITC computation, not in this definition) and is a common reference convention, so it is a minor deviation rather than an unsafe one — but it adds an element absent from the cited text.

[non-blocking] 'Net earnings from self-employment' is defined 'within the meaning of section 1402(a)'; the encoding uses a local input (`net_earnings_from_self_employment_determined_with_regard_to_section_164_f_deduction`) rather than importing the canonical 1402(a) definition. Acceptable for an isolated slice where 1402(a) may be unavailable, but an import would be preferable.

[non-blocking] The (B)(i) 'without regard to community property laws' rule applies to the entire earned income of the individual, but it is folded only into the employee-compensation input name and is not visibly applied to the self-employment term. Defensible as a modeling simplification, but slightly narrows the textual scope.

[non-blocking] `entity: TaxUnit` is a coherent EITC-context choice, though (B)(i) speaks of 'the earned income of an individual'; a Person-level base aggregated to the unit would track the text more literally. Non-blocking ontology nuance.

Over-deferral discards the bulk of an encodable definition. The module emits `rules: []` and defers everything, yet most of IRC §32(c)(2) does not depend on §1402(a) and is independently encodable now: the (A)(i) limb (wages, salaries, tips, and other employee compensation includible in gross income) and all six subparagraph (B) modifications — (B)(i) computed without regard to community property laws, (B)(ii) no pension/annuity, (B)(iii) no §871(a) nonresident-alien income, (B)(iv) no inmate-service income, (B)(v) no subsidized work-activity income under SSA 407(d)(4)/(7), and (B)(vi) the §112 election. None of these require net earnings from self-employment, so deferring them is a substantive loss of whole-rule fidelity (the rule's operative branches and exceptions are left entirely unencoded).

A normal cross-statute dependency is modeled as a hard blocker instead of an input/import. earned_income = includible employment compensation + net earnings from self-employment (per §1402(a), determined with regard to §164(f)). The §1402(a) term is a standard tax-unit/person annual monetary amount with no unsupported-ontology issue, and the file already knows its exact import URI (`us:statutes/26/1402/a#net_earnings_from_self_employment`). The correct pattern — and the rubric's own prescription for unavailable cited provisions — is to model that term as an imported input and encode the composition (wages limb + §164(f)-adjusted SE input − the (B) modifications + §112 election), not to defer the entire definition. Because the dependency is ontologically supported and only unencoded in-workspace, neither the `entity_not_supported` safe harbor nor the editorial-omission safe harbor applies to justify a blanket deferral.
